transcript.answer:
Only partly. Sending the token as the subprotocol keeps it out of the URL and the request line, so a URL-based access log won't capture it. It is not fully safe from logging. The token still travels in the request's Sec-WebSocket-Protocol header, so an ingress or proxy log that captures request headers, or a proxy trace, can record it. The old documented rationale, which said this avoids log exposure, was only half true (issue #150).

The response-side leak has been fixed. Previously the server echoed the token back in the 101 response headers and kept it on the socket object, where a debug console.log(ws) would print it. HAL Engine now offers and answers only the marker `hal.v1`, so the client offers `hal.v1, <token>`. The response carries `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol: hal.v1` and no token, and the socket's `protocol` is `hal.v1`. The issue's acceptance criteria also require that no offered subprotocol value is written to any log, including in the close handler. The docs are to list every place the credential exists, so operators can configure header redaction.

The remaining request-header exposure is something operators must handle by redacting that header in their logs. I did not read the final protocol doc wording itself.
sources: issue-150 (re-cinq/Otto #150: Stop echoing the access token in the WebSocket handshake response)

judgements.reason: The answer says it is not fully safe, explains that the server echoed the token into the 101 response headers, and describes the fix where the client offers hal.v1 first and the server selects that marker, all consistent with the gold answer.
